trigger: Lease abstraction and tenant reporting taking a week every month

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Ben Wallace, Sam from Eleno. Before I get into anything, are you still the director running the commercial management side at Ridgeline Commercial?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: That's me. Fifty-two people in Cremorne, and about two thirds of that is property management rather than sales. The thing I booked this call about is lease abstraction. It eats a week every month.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Tell me what that week actually looks like, hour by hour if you can?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: Two property analysts sit with a pile of lease documents and pull out the key terms. Commencement, expiry, rent review dates and mechanisms, outgoings recovery, make good, option periods. They type those into our management system and then build the tenant reports off the back of it.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: How many leases are moving through that in a month?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: New and varied, about forty. But the reporting covers the whole portfolio, which is around eleven hundred tenancies across three hundred assets. So it is not just the new ones, it is every review date and every outgoings reconciliation.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Where do the lease documents live and what state are they in?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: Mostly PDFs in our document management system, some scanned, some native. Quality varies a lot, especially anything inherited when we took over a portfolio. There are deeds of variation sitting as separate files that nobody has linked back to the head lease.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: What breaks when someone gets an abstraction wrong?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: A missed rent review is the expensive one. We had one last year where an option date passed and the tenant held over at the old rent for eighteen months. The owner was not delighted, and we wore part of it.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: And what would a good outcome look like to you, in a way your owners would notice?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: Reporting that goes out in a day instead of a week, no missed critical dates, and the two analysts spending their time on arrears and owner relationships rather than typing. If owners get their reports on the third of the month every month, that is something we can sell on a new mandate.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: So what we would build is a lease abstraction pipeline. It reads the lease and any variations, extracts the terms against a schema you define, flags anything it is not confident about for a human to check, and writes the confirmed terms into your management system. The tenant reports then generate from that.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: The flagging part is what I would want to press on. If it quietly guesses a rent review mechanism and gets it wrong, that is worse than the analyst typing it.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Agreed, and that is the design principle rather than a feature we added later. Every extracted term carries a confidence and a pointer to the clause it came from. Anything below threshold goes to a review queue instead of into the system. Your analysts become checkers on the hard ten per cent rather than typists on all of it.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: That I can sell internally. The analysts will not fight something that removes the boring eighty per cent.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: On numbers, a fixed-scope build for Ridgeline Commercial lands at $78,200, with a discovery phase of about three weeks first, where we run a sample of your real leases through and measure the extraction quality.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: Measuring on our own leases before we commit is the right way round. What does the discovery phase cost on its own?

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Six thousand for this scope, and it comes off the build if you proceed. I will send the discovery scope and the fixed build price by Thursday with the sample methodology attached.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: Thursday is fine. Send it to me and I will bring in our head of property management, because she owns the reporting calendar.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Can we book Friday 11 September at 9am with you and your head of property management to go through it?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: Friday 11 September at 9am works. She is in the office on Fridays anyway.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Good. I will also run twenty of your real leases through the extraction before that meeting, so we are looking at your numbers rather than a generic accuracy claim.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: Twenty is enough to show me whether it handles the messy inherited ones. Pick some from the portfolio we took on in Ballarat, they are the worst of it.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: I will ask for those specifically. If it struggles on scanned deeds of variation, better that we both know in September than in March.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: That is an honest answer. The last provider we looked at demonstrated on a clean template lease and would not touch ours.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: The other thing worth saying is that we deploy into your environment and transfer the intellectual property at handover. You are not renting this back from us forever.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: That matters on the owners' side as well. They ask who holds the data whenever we pitch for a new mandate.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Sam Whitfield
turns.text: Then we will cover data residency and ownership in the scope document, so you have an answer in writing rather than a verbal assurance.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Ben Wallace
turns.text: Thanks Sam. Thursday for the document, Friday for the meeting.
